I've come to the conclusion that using models of all but a few types to make practical decisions is scientifically illiterate.

I am not anti-science and in fact was studying as one for a while. What I learned is that scientists work with a spectrum of reliable information from entirely bullshit to universal and proven laws. This is their job to work with both and refine every part along the whole spectrum so that it all becomes closer to the proven laws side rather than the bullshit side. But all the interesting work is toward the bullshit side. This isn't to say anything negative about scientists but their job is mostly to work with bullshit.

And this has academic utility. You take a model prediction of the future. You watch it fail, because it was mostly bullshit. You figure out why it failed and what you could have done to improve it. You understand the world a little better by doing that. That's the product. Not the improved model, and not the first model, but the improvement of understanding the world that comes from it.

So it's not a scientists job to come up with useful or accurate models. It's to work with mostly bullshit models and figure out later why specifically they were bullshit and what that teaches us that we didn't know before.

There is a difference between a model for the future like climate models or epidemiological models vs models of kinetic movement. One has had hundreds of years of refinement. Even relatively recent refinement in the form of general relativity, and quantum mechanics if dealing with something small. On the other hand when people first started thinking about motion most of their theories were bullshit. But that was science. That is the scientific process.

So good scientific literacy is not to "always trust a scientist" or "always trust science." But to recognize accurately the degree of reliability that different scientific products can have. The majority of which are bullshit. And that's not a problem for science because the presence of bullshit in science is perfectly fine as long as the consumer of it is aware of that and understands that its presence is part of the scientific process.

But trust in science as a whole is undermined when people place undue assurance on unreliable models that should have never been used to make a decision, because their only real value is academic. And that's ok if we don't have idiots who can't understand that, or even worse, scientists who don't.
